papers.title: Fairness and incentives in combinatorial assignment
papers.abstract: We consider the fair and efficient random assignment of indivisible goods subject to resource constraints. Agents receive bundles randomly, but individual lotteries over bundles that are feasible in expectation need not be jointly feasible. Consequently, we treat a lottery over feasible allocations as a public good. We show that every feasible finite economy admits an envy-free and Pareto efficient random assignment that may be supported as a Lindahl equilibrium. For a finite type space with specified expected utilities, we construct a mechanism whose outcomes are exactly feasible and Pareto efficient with respect to reported preferences. As the population grows and empirical type proportions and per-capita resources approach a limiting large economy, envy and gains from manipulation vanish. The approximate incentive compatibility of the mechanism holds for all type profiles that approximate the limiting economy. The argument combines sensitivity bounds for linear programs with proximity bounds between fractional and integer optima.

papers.title: Contests versus Contracts in Innovation Procurement
papers.abstract: How much competition should a designer introduce when procuring innovation? We study a designer funding multiple technological approaches whose feasibility is learned through experimentation. Between independent contracts and contests, we introduce interdependent contracts, which combine approach-specific rewards with continuation decisions that depend on rivals' outcomes. When both breakthroughs and breakdowns are contractable, these contracts implement the optimum by extracting firms' rents and coordinating experimentation across approaches. When only breakthroughs are contractable, we compare simple mechanisms with constant contractual payments. Under technological symmetry, optimal interdependent contracts terminate experimentation at a success cutoff or deadline. Fixed-prize contests can implement the same innovation outcomes, but their relative expenditure depends on the experimentation horizon: for interior success cutoffs, contests are more expensive when the horizon is short and less expensive when it is sufficiently long. Rank-contingent contests can weakly outperform constant-payment interdependent contracts, but technological heterogeneity can reverse this ranking because individualized contracts better tailor incentives to different approaches. We further characterize optimal interdependent contracts with time-varying payments, extending the comparison beyond simple mechanisms. Our results show how outcome contractability, technological heterogeneity, and payment flexibility shape the desirable form of competition in innovation procurement.

papers.title: Privacy-Preserving Disclosure and Welfare
papers.abstract: We consider a monopolist selling to multiple buyers. A platform observes buyers' tastes and can publicly disclose information about those tastes. However, the platform faces a privacy constraint: the disclosure must reveal nothing about any individual buyer's taste. We show that the same pairs of consumer and producer surplus are attainable with or without this constraint. For each such pair, we construct a privacy-preserving disclosure rule under which a posted-price mechanism attains the pair and no other feasible selling mechanism earns more.

papers.title: What it is to Obey
papers.abstract: Prior to agents taking part in a simultaneous-move game, a designer commits a device that sends signals to each of the agents, evaluating the resulting set of equilibria according to a (Hausdorff-)continuous function. In games of incomplete information I show that it must be without loss of optimality for the designer to restrict attention to direct obedient devices if and only if she assumes her preferred equilibrium will be played. In games of complete information, I characterize the monotone evaluations, which include both the maximally optimistic one and the maximally pessimistic one.

papers.title: Credit Access and Mutual Risk Sharing
papers.abstract: A credit mutual shares project returns among its borrowers. Outside lenders finance borrowers the mutual turns away. As the mutual admits riskier projects, safer borrowers must contribute more to the pool. Beyond a threshold they leave. Borrowers who already had credit then lose as a group. If the gains to newly financed borrowers outweigh this loss at the threshold, opening the market continues to raise ex ante welfare after exit. Near full capacity, the original members lose from outside access even when the mutual offers safer borrowers enough to stay.

papers.title: The Gatekeeping Expert's Dilemma
papers.abstract: This paper studies how experts with veto power---gatekeeping experts---influence agents through communication. Their expertise informs agents' decisions, while veto power provides discipline. Gatekeepers face a dilemma: transparent communication can invite gaming, while opacity wastes expertise. How can gatekeeping experts guide behavior without being gamed? Many economic settings feature this tradeoff, including bank stress tests, environmental regulations, and financial auditing. Using financial auditing as the primary setting, I show that strategic vagueness resolves this dilemma: by revealing just enough to prevent the manager from inflating the report, the auditor guides the manager while minimizing opportunities for manipulation. This theoretical lens provides a novel rationale for why auditors predominantly accept clients' financial reports. Comparative statics reveal that greater gatekeeper independence or expertise sometimes dampens communication. This paper offers insights into why gatekeepers who lack direct control can still be effective.

papers.title: Individual Sovereignty and Other-Regarding Preferences
papers.abstract: We consider the social aggregation of preferences over lotteries in the presence of other-regarding preferences. If society respects each individual's sovereignty, an axiom we propose akin to Sen's Liberalism, then society's utility is a linear combination of individuals' self-regarding utilities. That is, other-regarding preferences can only influence the weights society places on each individual. We next characterize the unique weighting method under which society's weight ratio between two individuals is the geometric mean of those of all individuals. The central axiom requires that when only a group of individuals is at stake, society's preferences depend only on individuals' preferences towards that group. We extend the first result to a setting with feasibility constraints and to a setting with subjective uncertainty.

papers.title: Interpersonally Comparable Utility
papers.abstract: We develop a theory of measurement scales for utility functions, based on a generalization of the notion of numeraire commodity. Every sufficiently well-behaved utility is denominated in some scale of this form, and conversely, the choice of a compatible scale unit uniquely identifies utilities up to an additive constant. We define a profile of utilities to be interpersonally comparable precisely when they are denominated in a common measurement unit. We study when profiles of comparable utilities exist, as well as how a planner ought to aggregate them, and provide applications to social choice and welfare economics.

papers.title: Bins
papers.abstract: I characterize the undominated ways of transmitting, storing, and organizing information under capacity constraints, showing that they take a precise geometric form. Under a regularity assumption on the information to be organized, they are convex subdivisions of the space of beliefs constructed by recursively subdividing cells according to weighted proximity criteria.

papers.title: Strategy-proof interval aggregation
papers.abstract: A natural generalization of the voting problem on the real line is the collective choice of an interval, such as an interval forecast provided by experts, a range of permissible actions, the start and end times of an event, and the age range covered by a curriculum. For agents with single-peaked preferences over intervals, we introduce a broad family of Left-Right rules that generalizes the familiar Min-Max voting rules to interval choice. This family consists exactly of the peak-only strategy-proof rules, and its anonymous members coincide with the generalized median rules. Surprisingly, when the number $n$ of agents is odd, the ordinary median rule is the unique efficient, anonymous, and strategy-proof rule; when $n$ is even, no rule satisfies all three properties. Finally, a Left-Right rule is group strategy-proof if and only if it is one-sided or quasi-dictatorial.
